## Summary

Eisman argues that AI now dominates both incremental US growth and market exposure, making traditional diversification less reliable. He traces how his AI thesis changed as capital spending, model competition and customer pricing became more concerning, using his evolving subprime research as an analogy. He discloses stocks, cash and shorts as his portfolio framework.

Full transcript reviewed. Empirical claims without inspected primary outcome evidence remain unresolved; guest claims are separate from Eisman attribution. Primary outcome verification is incomplete for claims marked unresolved; these are not adverse accuracy grades.

## Framework and tools

- Theses develop through accumulating evidence rather than sudden certainty.
- Look through index and asset-class labels to common economic exposures.
- Demand durable moats and realized capital returns from large investment budgets.
- Use historical analogies to search for unrecognized risks, not merely headline opinions.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Apollo decomposition of 2026 GDP growth
- S&P technology weighting and AI-related corporate debt shares
- Hyperscaler capex budgets and capital raises
- Oracle backlog concentration
- Samsung earnings and share response

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman hosts the episode; guest turns are inferred from introductions and conversational context.
- An embedded Torsten Slok clip supplies the one-percentage-point AI growth estimate; Eisman then explicitly adopts it.
- The Oracle earnings quarter/month description is internally questionable and needs a filing timeline check.
- Token is described as roughly a word; actual tokenization varies.
- A 60/40 allocation does not specify whether bonds are Treasuries, corporate bonds or something else.
